messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Arguments: Arguments, Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir was eleven years old the first time he learned that the safest place in a room was the wall. His father’s hand had come across the dinner table without warning—not a slap, but a hard, flat strike to the side of Amir’s head that sent his vision white for a moment. The argument had been about nothing: a grade, a forgotten chore, a tone of voice Amir didn’t even remember using. What he remembered was the shock of being touched, the way his mother’s face crumpled as she tried not to cry, and the certainty that any moment of disagreement could turn into a blow. Over the years that followed, the pattern became as predictable as gravity. A raised voice meant flinch. A sudden hand near his shoulder meant freeze. And crying—whether his mother’s silent tears after an incident, or later, anyone else’s—meant something was terribly, dangerously wrong.

Now nineteen, married for just over a year, and working as an environmental scientist for a small consulting firm, Amir had built a life that looked steady from the outside. But the internal architecture of that life was entirely defensive. In the office he chose his desk second, after watching where his coworkers sat—always the corner desk with his back to the wall, his line of sight open to the door and every face that entered. When he met with clients, he arrived early to seat himself at the far end of the conference table, or positioned himself against a bookshelf. He had come to believe that he could read danger in a furrowed brow, a too-quick exhale, a gaze that lingered a half-second too long. This scanning had become automatic, almost exhausting, but letting it go felt like taking off a helmet in a war zone.

At home, his wife Leila had begun to notice that he left the room whenever she started to cry—whether from a sad movie or a stressful phone call. He never said why; he only knew that the sound of it made his chest tighten and his feet move toward the door. Arguments were worse. When he felt a disagreement coming, even about something small like whose turn it was to do the grocery shopping, Amir would go silent, agree too quickly, or physically leave the house. He had never told Leila that the last time he’d argued with his father, he’d ended up with a cracked rib. She only knew that her husband seemed to disappear whenever things got hard.

Avoiding people was simpler. He had no close friends at work, no one he met for coffee. He took his lunch at his desk or in his car, and he scheduled field sampling days so he could be alone in the wetlands he monitored, away from colleagues. But that solitude brought its own terror: being alone in an empty building or a quiet stretch of marsh made his skin prickle. He was certain that in an open, unguarded space, something could come at him from any direction. So he kept his phone on, kept his back to a tree when he stopped, and never stayed late at the office if he could help it.

The cost of these habits had become visible. His supervisor had noted that he seemed “hard to collaborate with” and had put him on solo projects. Leila had started sleeping on the far side of the bed after waking one night to find Amir rigid, his eyes open, his arm locked across his chest as though bracing for a blow. She had been reaching out to touch his shoulder—something he’d told her he hated, being touched without warning—and he had jerked away so violently he hit his head on the headboard.

What finally brought Amir to a therapist’s office was not a single crisis but a slow erosion. He was tired of scanning faces, of feeling safe only in corners, of watching his wife’s confusion turn into frustration. He wanted to believe that a disagreement could end without harm, that crying didn’t mean someone was about to be hurt, that he could sit in the middle of a room and still breathe. He came because he was afraid that if he didn’t learn a different way to live, he would lose the marriage he had fought to build—and because, for the first time in years, he was willing to let someone see the fear he carried.
